"With so much noise about AI taking away everyone's jobs, his perspective is practical, honest, and grounded in common sense."

"Here are 4 simple takeaways that stood out to me:"
"1. Don't fall for the "Job Apocalypse" panic"
""
"A lot of the fear in the news is hyped up to grab headlines or help big tech companies look more powerful than they actually are. In reality, when tools make developers faster, companies actually end up wanting to build more things—meaning more demand for engineers. The real work isn't worrying about doom scenarios; it's learning how to build with these new tools."
""
"2. Think beyond just "cutting costs""
""
"Many leaders still view AI purely as a way to reduce headcount or save a few pennies. But the bigger opportunity is using it to build better products, serve customers faster, and grow the business. Cost savings have a limit; growth does not."
""
"3. Doing the task isn't the same as learning"
""
"Andrew shared an important warning here: using a chatbot to do your homework or finish a task gets the job done, but it doesn't teach your brain how to think. Relying on AI for everything without understanding the basics actually hurts long-term skill. Use AI to assist your work, not to replace your thinking."
""
"4. A tool is still just a tool"
""
"An AI agent does not have free will. If someone swings a hammer and breaks a wall, we blame the person holding the hammer—not the tool itself. The responsibility stays with the humans designing and using these systems."
"Technology is moving fast, but success still comes down to the basics: keep learning, focus on solving real problems, and don't get distracted by the noise."

"AI doesn’t fail because the models aren't intelligent enough—it fails because it lacks context."
""
"Karthik Raman points out that we are entering a new era of AI engineering where Context is the New Code. "
""
"Instead of hardcoding every rule and pipeline, we now provide context to help autonomous AI agents reason, plan, and orchestrate tools."
""
"To make this work at an enterprise scale, you need to master these 5 Dimensions of Context "
""
"1️⃣ Business Context "
"What does the data actually mean? Without a semantic model encoding business rules, formulas, and filters, AI might generate a perfectly valid SQL query that calculates the completely wrong answer for your business."
""
"2️⃣ Technical Context"
"How is the data structured? Details like column types, joins, partition keys, and data freshness timestamps help AI agents autonomously decide the most efficient way to retrieve your data."
""
"3️⃣ Trust Context"
"What is the AI allowed to see? This is where many AI projects fail. Robust security features and data masking must define access boundaries before the data ever reaches the model. Governance is not an afterthought!"
""
"4️⃣ Operational Context"
"What is the current state of the system? Agents need to be aware of query latency, pipeline failures, and task histories to power proactive, autonomous behavior (like alerting users if a morning ETL job fails)."
""
"5️⃣ Domain Context"
"What are the specific rules of your industry? Whether it's healthcare regulations, financial compliance, or manufacturing standards, domain knowledge ensures the AI operates safely within your specific industry parameters."
""
"The ultimate takeaway: If you want to move your GenAI projects out of the demo phase and into production, invest heavily in your semantic models and governance framework today! "

"I recently listened to a talk by Stanford CS Professor Chris Piech on the reality of learning to program in the age of generative AI."
""
"As a Data and AI enthusiast, I appreciate his perspective because it cuts through the current hype with cold numbers and historical patterns. Here are the core data points and realities he highlighted:"
""
"**1. AI tutors are not a silver bullet**"
"In Stanford’s *Code in Place* program (17,000+ students), throwing chatbots at learners predictably caused dropouts and demotivation. However, when an actual human instructor popped in for just a 10-minute check-in, the course completion probability jumped by 10 percentage points. The AI was factually correct, but it lacks the human capacity to ignite curiosity or contextually inspire."
""
"**2. We grossly overestimate the speed of total automation**"
"Piech points to the self-driving car milestones of 2011–2012. At that time, experts predicted the immediate demise of truck drivers. Instead, the profession grew. Why? Because humans consistently overestimate how fast AI can master the final "1% long-tail" of messy, chaotic real-world edge cases."
""
"**3. Syntax is cheap; Architecture and Problem-Solving are expensive**"
"Programming consists of two distinct parts: syntax (memorizing commands) and problem-solving (system architecture and data structure). AI will master syntax completely. If you outsource your foundational coding entirely to Claude or Cursor today, you will lose the cognitive friction required to understand architecture. Five weeks down the line, when your prototype breaks in production under actual user load, you will not know how to fix the bugs."
""
"**The takeaway for engineers:**"
"The barrier to entry has dropped. An 18-year-old can now spin up a functional codebase using AI. Because execution is democratized, the high-order skill is no longer rote coding. The top engineers will be those who master the interface between human problems and data systems—figuring out exactly *what* is worth building in the first place."
"Use the tool to build prototypes, but demand it to teach you *how* it built them. Don't skip the foundations."

"1. The Blueprint vs. The Quick Fix (Don't Build in a Vacuum)"
"When companies build new tech (like data systems or AI), they usually make one of two mistakes: they spend millions building a massive system before proving it works, or they build tiny, isolated projects that don't talk to each other. The trick is to do both at the same time: pick a real, immediate problem, solve it quickly, and make sure the tools you built to solve it can be reused for the next project."
""
"2. The Danger of Cutting Corners"
"There is always a fight between doing something fast to make one boss happy and doing it right for the whole company. If you cut corners just to get a quick win, you create "technical debt"—which is like charging a quick fix to a high-interest credit card. Eventually, you end up with a messy web of broken, unorganized systems that cost a fortune to clean up later."
""
"3. Good Ingredients Make Good Food"
"Whether you are doing basic math, data science, or advanced AI, your results are only as good as the data you put in. Instead of cleaning up messy data for every single new project, smart companies build "data products"—clean, organized, reusable packages of information (like a master file of everything about a customer). Once you have these high-quality ingredients ready, building new projects becomes faster, cheaper, and easier."
""

""
" * Context Explosion: The rapid, unwanted growth of the agent's message history."
" * Context Rot: The resulting drop in LLM performance, stability, and speed as the context window becomes too large."
" * Pre-Rot Threshold: The token limit (e.g., 128K–200K) used as a trigger for reduction techniques before degradation begins."
" * KV Cache (Key-Value Cache): A performance feature that stores and reuses embeddings for common prefixes (like system prompts) to reduce cost and latency."
" * Context Confusion: When too many tools are defined in the context, causing the agent to call the wrong ones."
" * Context Offloading: Moving token-heavy data (like raw tool outputs) out of the active context into external storage."
" * Compaction (Reversible Reduction): Stripping redundant data while keeping light-weight references (like file paths) in the history, used as the first step of context reduction."
" * Structured Summarization: Using schemas (defined forms) instead of free-form prompts to ensure high-recall information is preserved when context is summarized."
" * Layered Action Space: Organizing tools into tiers (atomic functions, sandbox utilities, APIs) to minimize the number of tool definitions in the core context."
" * Agent as Tool: Using a sub-agent to handle complex, specialized tasks (like advanced search or planning) and return only a final, clean output to the main agent."
" * Context Isolation: Splitting the task environment across specialized sub-agents to achieve a separation of concerns and prevent context clutter."

The reason the perceptron was exciting was that it could learn to classify images without having the shapes of letters manually programmed into it. ""As AI systems become more capable, we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs. We experiment with methods for training a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement, without any human labels identifying harmful outputs. The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles, and so we refer to the method as 'Constitutional AI'. The process involves both a supervised learning and a reinforcement learning phase. In the supervised phase we sample from an initial model, then generate self-critiques and revisions, and then finetune the original model on revised responses. In the RL phase, we sample from the finetuned model, use a model to evaluate which of the two samples is better, and then train a preference model from this dataset of AI preferences. We then train with RL using the preference model as the reward signal, i.e. we use 'RL from AI Feedback' (RLAIF). As a result we are able to train a harmless but non-evasive AI assistant that engages with harmful queries by explaining its objections to them. Both the SL and RL methods can leverage chain-of-thought style reasoning to improve the human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making. These methods make it possible to control AI behavior more precisely and with far fewer human labels.""

"IBM watsonx.governance can be utilized to measure the RAG Triad metrics: Context Relevance, Faithfulness, and Answer Relevance."
"Context Relevance: This measures whether the retrieved contexts are pertinent to the question"
"Faithfulness: This assesses whether the model is deriving the answer from the provided context or if it is being creative and providing its own answer, which could lead to hallucinations."
"Answer Relevance: This evaluates whether the obtained answer is relevant to the question"
"Here is a quick description of additional metrics:"
"Answer Similarity Metric: This metric assesses the overall semantic similarity between the generated response and the ideal answer"
"Answer Coverage Metrics: These include various measures:"
"Coverage: Evaluates how much of the answer is a derivative of the context"
"Density: Measures how closely the answer follows the source text"
"Compression: Assesses the conciseness of the generated summary compared to the source"
"Novelty: Evaluates the presence of new n-grams in the answer compared to the references"
"Redundancy: Detects repetitive information within the answer"
"Keyword Inclusions: Checks for the presence of important keywords from the context in the answer and calculates the F1 Score for matching keywords between the context and the answer"
"Unanswered Questions: Identifies questions that the model could not answer"

"Listen – One of the most important traits for a leader. I learnt from a workshop that I attended that it is important to be an active listener. One of the tricks of an active listener is that he makes notes (physical or mental) during the conversation and uses points from that while he makes his point. It is very difficult to keep our minds concentrated on what we are listening to if we are not genuine about the listening. I practice this and this has given its dividends. Sometime back I was given the opportunity of presenting my project to the customer. I was to speak about my project for half an hour, however the speaker before me was a master in his skill and an excellent orator. He kept the audience captivated and overshot the time and all I got was 5 minutes. I had to make my mark in those 5 minutes. I had made my notes while the customer was speaking. I had a list of concerns that they were facing in their current system. Luckily my project was solving similar concerns for my customer. All I did in those 5 minutes was link his concerns to how my project was solving my customer’s problems. I linked each of the features of my projects to the notes that I had taken and quoted the customer often. They liked it very much and I heard later that they even told the Chairman of my company that they were impressed with my capability to relate to their business challenges. This would not have been possible without active listening. The trap that most of us fall into is that we are waiting to make our point once the other person has closed his/her mouth, so we do not really listen to others, one of the ways of overcoming this is to note down our thoughts and continue listening to others. One of the managers I had worked with had this reputation of not being a good listener and I learnt it the hard way what it feels when your manager does not listen to you. It pays to improve one’s listening skills.
